b: A fawning love letter to macho, turn-of-the-’70s Hollywood, Quentin Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time…in Hollywood was structured and marketed around the Manson family murders, the latest target of the filmmaker’s revisionist revenge fantasies. In Tarantino’s telling, the Manson acolytes who in real life murdered Sharon Tate were self-righteous hippies bent on tarnishing classic Hollywood’s golden-hued legacy, and so, rather than carry out their infamous crime, they had their faces caved in by Cliff Booth (Brad Pitt). A hard-bitten stuntman and WWII vet, Cliff is exactly the kind of morally dubious tough guy that Tarantino adores, albeit one nagged by questions about his relevance in an aging body and a changing society.

Cliff gets the spotlight all to himself in David Fincher’s The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, which, save for one brief, bittersweet cameo, leaves the rest of Once Upon a Time…in Hollywood’s ensemble behind. It’s the first feature Tarantino has scripted for another director since Robert Rodriguez’s From Dusk Till Dawn 30 years ago, and as the product of the mutual admiration society of Fincher, Tarantino, and Pitt, it’s a surprisingly liberated film, freed from the white-elephantine pressures of Tarantino’s solo authorial brand. At once among the mellowest and most distressing entries in both Fincher’s and Tarantino’s filmographies, it finds in the aftermath of a midlife crisis a humbler, more sobering acceptance of life, aging, death, and the movies, without fully abandoning a puckish sense of fun.

In 1977, eight years after he carved up members of the Manson family in the home of his friend and former employer, Rick Dalton, Cliff’s life has become less glamorous, not more. Rick never became the movie star he dreamed of being, but he did land a steady gig on a TV show in Australia, leading to an amicable parting of ways with his longtime partner in mischief. Lacking regular stunt work in Rick’s absence, Cliff zips between odd jobs across a Los Angeles that’s as dingy and nocturnal through the lenses of Fincher and cinematographer Erik Messerschmidt as it was coated in a late-summer glow through those of Tarantino and Robert Richardson.

As a fixer and liaison between the American movie business’s glamorous veneer and its seedy underbelly, Cliff’s duties range from mixing drinks at a mud-wrestling bar and manning the projection booth at the New Beverly Cinema (which Tarantino has owned since 2007) to recovering stolen Oscars, mediating criminal payment disputes, and committing the occasional murder at the behest of wealthy studio talent. When he isn’t on the clock or mingling with celebrities on the periphery of sleaze, Cliff holes up in the bachelor pad he shares with his elderly father, Gus (Peter Weller), tending to his model planes and his spoiled cat. Weller, his voice as commanding as ever at age 79, nails a tightrope walk between crotchety and endearing.

An underworld legend kept narrowly out of the daylight, Cliff is tailed by a past that he seems neither lost in nor afraid of. Everyone wants to hear his Hollywood tales and stories of heroism in the Pacific, but he lives firmly in the present. Freed from Once Upon a Time…in Hollywood’s buddy-comedy hijinks, in which he was the yang to Rick’s yin, the film—which marries Tarantino’s hard-boiled, digressive dialogue to Fincher’s interest in methodical, lonely men on the fringes of social acceptability—allows us to simply live with this workaday character.

The film takes its sweet time between its promised misadventures, which are refreshingly low-stakes and separated by intertitles that mark the passing hours, often with a snarky punchline. As in Once Upon a Time…in Hollywood, there’s plenty of format-authentic footage of kitschy TV shows and movies within the movie, accompanied by made-up Hollywood trivia that’s sometimes narrated by Tarantino. Shot and cut with Fincher’s needling noir precision rather than Tarantino’s carnivalesque energy, the film gradually fills in and humanizes Pitt’s half-empty well of grinning machismo when he isn’t menacing mouthy ne’er-do-wells at gunpoint.

Cliff’s more vulnerable side emerges in the clouding of his eyes and the swelling of his voice when he recalls his time in the Pacific, runs into an old lover, gazes at mementos from Rick, chats with his dad over TV broadcasts, or merely sighs in resignation at the never-ending complications of his life in the shadows. Eventually, a plot takes shape: Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), a popular star known for doing his own stunts and a Cliff Booth superfan, enlists Cliff’s help with a sticky situation involving his hot-and-cold marriage to actress Toni (Carla Gugino) and a pair of Filipino mafiosi, Eddie (Matt Groove) and Fernando Verdusco (JB Tadena). (A possible nod to Breaking Bad’s Salamanca twins, the brothers cover a spectrum from affable to terrifying that’s as pronounced as Christoph Waltz’s in Inglourious Basterds.)

This setup provides as much genre intrigue as it does an opportunity for Cliff to court Charlie’s statuesque blond agent, Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), in a strangely sweet romance that reveals the chisel-cut tough guy and rumored wife-killer to be a sexual masochist, yearning less for penetration than for a strong woman’s slap in the face. And that gives Fincher and Tarantino an excuse for Karen—a former film critic and disciple of Tarantino’s critical idol, Pauline Kael—to launch into withering, podcast-ready musings on the relationship between trash, art, and commerce in American cinema. Her monologues are subtly underlined by the looming presence of Star Wars over the 1977 setting: a post-kitsch passion project from a New Hollywood auteur that would unwittingly reshape the industry, ushering in a corporatized, blockbuster-oriented business model at the expense of the scrappier, edgier films of Tarantino’s beloved ’70s.

Amid a host of discursive asides and cheeky running gags (Cliff is endlessly asked, “Do I know you from somewhere?”), one standout thread is Charlie’s troubling confusion of play violence with the real thing. He constantly pleads with Cliff to teach him what taking a human life actually looks, sounds, and feels like, and he seems dangerously drawn to playing with death for real. Yet the difference between play and reality when blood hits the floor has never been rendered as searingly through Tarantino’s lens as it is through Fincher’s.

The film’s scenes of violence are relatively few, but their ice-cold chill radiates over everything. They’re ugly and clumsy, shot in static, middle-distance long takes with few merciful cutaways as bodies are battered, bent, and violated, their mechanical, sickening realism more redolent of Fincher’s past forays into true-crime forensics than of Tarantino’s love of exploitation hysteria. A home invasion by the Verdusco brothers—the most emotionally distressing scene in Tarantino’s entire filmography, and arguably in Fincher’s—contains no ironic one-liners or fevered crash zooms as an entire family is slain with unfeeling professionalism.

Even Cliff’s inevitable return to the saddle for righteous bloodshed drops any hint of Once Upon a Time…in Hollywood’s sadistic hippie-mulching glee. In its place are a nerve-shredding tension, accentuated by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross’s angrily droning score, and an excruciating awareness of its hero’s fallibility and mortality that’s wholly absent from the earlier film. It’s an eye-opening new take on violence in the Tarantinoverse: no longer a flip thrill, but a frightening reality and self-annihilating duty creeping up on these tragicomic wisecrackers and the charmed cynicism of their aging, movie-centric lives.

The severity of that violence, and the absence of any tidy catharsis, recasts the rest of the film’s loose, at times baggy shit-shooting meander as both somber and vital, the petty conflicts and trivial textures of living made more valuable, not less, by the looming glare of true evil and death. Bringing out new comic dimensions in Fincher and new tragic ones in Tarantino, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is a more haunting and far more mature film than Once Upon a Time…in Hollywood, and one of the most fruitful pairings of two highly distinct name-brand filmmakers since A.I. Artificial Intelligence.
